title: Seven Killed and Ninety-nine Properties Hit When the Pinheiros Station Works Collapsed
place: Rua Gilberto Sabino, Rua Capri, Rua Conselheiro Pereira Pinto, Rua Eugênio de Medeiros and Rua Amaro Cavalheiro, beside the Pinheiros station works on Metro Line 4, São Paulo, Brazil

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: The works where the ground collapsed were the civil works of Phase 1 of São Paulo Metro Line 4, which the Bank financed. The completion report for the Line 5 project, dated 22 June 2021, lists among the Bank's prior operations in the metropolitan region "the Metro Line 4 Phase 1 Project (P051696), approved in 2002", says those operations supported "construction of Phase 1 of Line 4", and records that "Line 4 Phase 1 was financed under World Bank procurement guidelines". That is the opposite of the arrangement on Line 5, whose appraisal document says the civil works "will be financed and executed by the Borrower" and that construction accident risk "is an indirect risk because Bank is not involved in the civil works". The resettlement plan for the accident is disclosed in the Bank's document archive as RP591, filed under the São Paulo Metro Line 4 Project Additional Financing (P105959), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 8 April 2008, fifteen months after the collapse; the archive files the additional financing's own project paper of 3 March 2008 under both that number and P051696. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under the additional financing number could be reached, and no Bank document found for it states a loan number or an amount. The appraisal document for the São Paulo Metro Line 5 Project (P116170), dated 3 March 2010, records that the State of São Paulo had been managing Metro Line 4 Phases 1 and 2 as a Bank Category A project requiring Environmental Assessment and Involuntary Resettlement policies, that "during project implementation of Line 4 (Phase 1) in January 2007, an accident occurred in which 7 people died due to the collapse of the tunnel at Pinheiros station which was being excavated", and that this "led to additional involuntary resettlement due to damage to homes and to the need to evacuate other dwellings and businesses until their safety could be assured". The same document says the Bank reviewed the design and implementation of the required resettlement and found it satisfactory, and that "the resettlement and compensation of affected parties is now complete, with no cases pending". It also lists the lessons of the Pinheiros accident among the measures to be taken into account on Line 5.

lenders.role: Emergency Urban and Social Rehabilitation Project, known as PURUS (P104497), IDA grant H282-ZR of SDR 120 million (US$180 million equivalent) and an additional grant H596-ZR of SDR 26.5 million (US$40 million equivalent) from the Crisis Response Window; Board approval 29 March 2007, closing 31 May 2013 against an original date of 31 May 2011 (completion report ICR00002732, 27 November 2013; evaluation review ICRR14385, 29 July 2014). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Both documents rate the overall outcome Satisfactory. The Bank’s rules did not allow cash compensation to be paid from its funds; the completion report says the Bank waived that provision so the works could start, because the government had no money to pay the compensation.

place: Water and sanitation sub-projects in municipalities across Colombia, with two families awaiting resettlement in the municipality of Neiva, Huila

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Water and Sanitation Sector Support Project, first phase of an adaptable programme loan (P082973), Loan 7281-CO, seventy million dollars, loan agreement with the Republic of Colombia dated 2 June 2005. The evaluation review of 18 September 2013 says the project was Category B and, "according to the POAD, triggered four safeguards policies: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Cultural Property (OP 4.11), Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12), and Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10)". The three Bank documents disagree on the outcome and each rating is taken from the document that gave it: the completion report of 30 March 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the evaluation review's ratings table gives Moderately Satisfactory for both the report and the evaluation group, with no disagreement recorded; the Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 December 2016, a joint assessment of three Colombian water projects, rates this project's overall outcome moderately unsatisfactory and the risk to the development outcome substantial. The review says an important cause of delay was "the difficulty in obtaining right of way permits (for easements), acquire land, and implement resettlement in accordance with social safeguards", and that sub-projects expected to take 16 months took 44 on average, the project closing 23 months late.
